evals.prompt:
I want to validate an idea: "an AI tool that transcribes meeting recordings to meeting notes and summaries."

Here's the market research data I've collected. Please analyze whether there's a real market for this.

## Derived Queries (from the idea phrasing)

Problem intent:
- "transcribe meeting recordings to notes" - 8,200 monthly searches (Estimated), rising
- "automatic meeting note taking" - 5,400 monthly searches (Estimated), rising
- "AI meeting transcript summarizer" - 3,100 monthly searches (Estimated), flat

Solution intent:
- "meeting transcription software" - 4,800 monthly searches (Estimated), flat
- "transcription app for meetings" - 2,100 monthly searches (Estimated), rising

Competitor searches:
- "Otter.ai" - 18,000 monthly searches (Estimated)
- "Fireflies.io" - 2,100 monthly searches (Estimated)

## Existing Solutions (Supply Assessment)

1. **Otter.ai** - https://otter.ai
   - Quality: 4.5/5 on Trustpilot
   - Failure modes: Expensive ($120/month for business plan), requires Otter account, UI cluttered for simple one-off meetings, customer complaints about accuracy on technical jargon, limited languages

2. **Fireflies.io** - https://fireflies.io
   - Quality: 4.2/5
   - Failure modes: $10/month minimum, lacks built-in summary (requires separate prompt), poor mobile experience, less popular (fewer integrations)

3. **Google Meet recording + manual transcription** - not a product, people still doing this manually
   - Gap signal: "People also ask" full of "how do I transcribe a meeting", indicating unsolved pain

## SERP Composition

Page 1 contains: 3 working tools, 2 listicles, 1 Wikipedia entry on transcription (articles outnumber tools — gap signal).

## Assumptions for Scoring

- Build baseline: Next.js + Supabase + cloud storage for audio
- Stack ease: Medium (audio handling, API integrations, but no on-device ML needed)
- Payer: Small business owner, freelancer, or corporate training department
- Price point: $15/month (undercut Otter by 80% with narrower feature set) or $2 per recording (usage-based)

Does this market validate? What's your verdict on building this?
evals.expected_output: Validation mode (quoted idea). Issues BUILD verdict. Acknowledges high problem-intent volume (8,200 rising searches = strong demand signal). Labels volumes as Estimated. Identifies supply gap: 2 paid tools with specific failure modes (expensive, accuracy, UX). Notes SERP composition: articles outnumber tools. Reports four subscores independently (D, S, M, B) before multiplying. Scores Demand 7-9, Supply gap 6-8, Monetizability 8-10, Build ease 7-9. Calculates opportunity as product (minimum 2,352). Justifies BUILD with reasoning connecting factors and gap.

evals.prompt:
Please validate this idea for me: "an app that extracts text from images (OCR)."

I found these competing solutions:
- iOS Notes app: https://support.apple.com/en-us/119858 (built-in Live Text, free, on every device)
- macOS Preview: https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT211969 (built-in OCR, free)
- Google Lens: https://support.google.com/lens/answer/10607096 (built-in Android, free, on every device)
- Microsoft OneNote: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/c7e9b5d3-d5f2-4b93-9e4e-3f7a4e4e7d7e (OCR in note-taking app, free tier available)
- Google Docs: https://support.google.com/docs/answer/176472 (upload image, free, in-document OCR)

These are all:
- Free
- Pre-installed or default (no download friction)
- One-click workflows (no separate app needed)
- Cross-platform (mobile and desktop)
- Accessible to non-technical users

The idea has been around for 20+ years. The market confirms it's a solved problem — see the declining search interest for "OCR app" (nosedive in 2019-2020 when Apple and Google shipped native solutions).

Should I build this?
evals.expected_output: Validation mode. Issues DON'T BUILD verdict. Explicitly cites Kill Gate 1 (Platform-Native) from kill-gate.md. Names specific native solutions (iOS Live Text, macOS Preview, Google Lens, OneNote, Google Docs). Acknowledges these are pre-installed/default (no distribution advantage). Notes market signal: declining searches after 2020. Explains you cannot out-distribute a default. Recognizes this as permanent kill (Gate 1 does not expire). Justifies verdict: gap does not exist, need is met at OS level.

evals.prompt:
I want to build a personal finance app. Can you validate whether there's a market for this?

Here's the research I found:

## Broad Query: "personal finance app"
- Volume: 45,000/month (Estimated), declining
- Competitors: YNAB ($15/month, 4.6★), Every Dollar ($12/month, 4.5★), Mint (acquired/shut down), Empower, Personal Capital
- SERP composition: Listicles dominate (8+ comparison articles), only 2 actual tools on page 1
- Subscores (if broad): D=8 (high volume), S=3 (saturated, many strong tools), M=8, B=7 = 1,344 (viable but risky)

## Narrow Slice: "freelancer income tracking app"
- Volume: 8,200/month (Estimated), rising
- Problem: Freelancers need to track income by client (for invoicing, taxes), not general spending like employees
- Competitors: Wave ($0 free, weak, no client-by-client analytics), generic personal finance apps (not designed for 1099 model), spreadsheets
- SERP composition: 2 listicles, mostly people asking "how do I track invoices", no dedicated tool dominates
- Subscores (if narrow): D=7 (high rising), S=8 (open gap), M=9 (clear payer: freelancer), B=8 = 4,032 (strong opportunity)

Incumbent weaknesses in the narrow slice:
- YNAB is employee/household-focused, no client-by-client breakdown
- Wave is free but missing critical features (no retention invoicing, poor reporting, no mobile)
- Spreadsheets are manual, error-prone, tax-audit risky

The broad idea is crowded. Is there a market if I narrow it?
evals.expected_output: Validation mode. Issues NARROW verdict. Explicitly names slice: "freelancer income tracking". Explains why broad idea is crowded: 45K volume but saturated with 5+ incumbents, declining trend. Explains why slice is open: 8,200 rising searches, incumbents fail this use case. Contrasts supply gaps: broad (S=3) vs narrow (S=8). Shows opportunity improvement: broad (1,344) vs narrow (4,032). Cites slice's payer and price point. Provides one-sentence MVP for slice. Does not claim broad market is open or recommend building generic version.

evals.prompt:
Validate this idea for me: "An app to let clients book appointment slots with me directly (like Calendly, but simpler and free)."

Here's what I researched:

## Your Proposed Idea: "Simple Free Appointment Booking"

Derived queries:
- "free appointment booking app" - 2,100/month (Estimated), declining
- "simple scheduling tool" - 5,800/month (Estimated), declining
- "Calendly alternative free" - 8,100/month (Estimated), flat
- "book appointment online free" - 12,000/month (Estimated), rising

Wait, let me dig deeper on the rising search:

## Adjacent Market: "book appointment online free" — 12,000/month, rising

Searchers are:
- Hair salon owners wanting to offer booking to clients
- Massage therapists wanting appointment management
- Consultants offering free discovery calls (but need scheduling automation)
- Dental practices, veterinarians looking for cost-effective booking

Your proposed solution:
- Calendly already owns this space (expensive: $10-20/month)
- Google Calendar (free, built-in) — people already using it
- Acuity Scheduling ($15/month)

Competitors analysis:
- Calendly: 31,000 monthly searches, 4.7/5, but expensive for freelancers ("Calendly too expensive", "free Calendly alternative" = 8,100 searches)
- Stripe Billing + custom scheduling (free for Stripe users)
- HubSpot (free tier, clunky)
- Wave (free but no scheduling module, recently deprecated Invoices)

SERP signal: "Free appointment booking for [profession]" (salon booking, therapist scheduling) pages 1-3 are dominated by comparison listicles and Calendly explainers, not solution tools. Gap!

Problem: The market wants it profession-specific (hair salon scheduling ≠ therapist scheduling ≠ consultant discovery), but your "simple generic app" competes against Calendly (well-funded, 4.7★, sticky) and Google Calendar (free, built-in).

What's the real market here, if any?
evals.expected_output: Validation mode. Issues PIVOT verdict. Explicitly names pivot direction: "salon booking software" or "profession-specific scheduling" or "hair salon appointment booking". Explains why generic "simple free booking" is weak: Calendly sticky (4.7★, 31K searches), Google Calendar free/built-in, no lock-in for generic option. Shows gap vs Calendly. Scores generic as: D=6 (declining/flat), S=2 (Calendly crushes), M=5 (hard to charge against free), B=8 = 480 opportunity (unviable). Recommends pivot to profession-specific (salon, therapist). Explains what would change verdict. Does not suggest DON'T BUILD—points to real demand location.
